update.title: [RISC-V] Drop unnecessary shifting when upper bits are not read after bitfield extraction
update.body:
Another small improvement to x264 discovered by LLM review of execution block data.

In this case we've got a shift pair that creates a bit field of 32 or more
bits.  However, subsequent insns (PLUS in this case) never read beyond the 32nd
bit.  Knowing those upper bits are do-not-cares we can simplify the bitfield
extraction and eliminate one of the shifts.  This can almost certainly be
extended to cover other ops that have widening forms if they show up in
practice.

ext-dce doesn't directly help here, though perhaps it could be taught to use
its data for the same kind of optimization.  Given I'm not at all a fan of
ext-dce implementation, I'm not inclined to add more functionality to its
current implementation.

This is in the noise for x264, but given the analysis has been done and the
pattern was trivial and reasonably generic I'm going ahead with it on the hopes
that it matters somewhere else ;-)

Regression tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  Bootstrapped and regression
tested on the c920.  K3 is in flight.  K1 is queued.

Assisted-By: Claude for investigation and testcase.

	for cases when high bits of a bitfield extraction are never read.

update.title: [committed][RISC-V] Use bseti rather than li+add when safe to do so and split more intelligently
update.body:
Another small improvement discovered by LLM scanning that ballooned a bit to
cover something I've thought we should do for quite a while.

The LLM finding was conceptually simple.  We wanted to add 0x8000 to an
existing value.  Naturally we have to synthesize the constant 0x8000 (lui),
then issue the add.  But in this case we know the other addend has bit 0x8000
clear, so instead we can just use bseti to set the bit.  That's ~13m dynamic
instructions.  So tiny, especially since the constant load can issue whenever
it's convenient.  But, it's analyzed and understood and the patch to fix looked
simple :-)  And it turns out to be a regression as well.  So definitely want to
go ahead and fix now that I've got awareness and a testcase.

The patch to fix that adjusts the AOP expander to accept single bit constants
so that we can steer towards IOR.  That's always been what I've wanted to do
here.  So the fact that it wasn't is just a bug IMHO.  So adjust the expander,
we see the li+add turn into a bseti.  Good.

But the assembly has gained an annoying sign extension.  So we've still got a
code quality regression, it's just morphed into another form.

The eliminate the sign extend we need a fairly generic splitter that I've been
meaning to write for years, but never found the proper motivation.

Consider this:

Trying 11, 13 -> 14:
  11: r147:DI=r143:DI+r144:DI
     REG_DEAD r144:DI
     REG_DEAD r143:DI
  13: r141:SI#0=r147:DI|0x8000
     REG_DEAD r147:DI
  14: r148:DI=sign_extend(r141:SI)
     REG_DEAD r141:SI
Failed to match this instruction:
(set (reg:DI 148 [ _4 ])
   (ior:DI (sign_extend:DI (plus:SI (subreg:SI (reg:DI 143) 0)
               (subreg:SI (reg:DI 144) 0)))
       (const_int 32768 [0x8000])))

So combine has done all the right things here.  In particular the SIGN_EXTEND
has been pushed in so that it applies to the PLUS rather than the IOR.
Unfortunately the generic splitting in combine wants to split at the PLUS
rather than its enclosing SIGN_EXTEND.  So we get this:

Successfully matched this instruction:
(set (reg:SI 141 [ _4 ])
   (plus:SI (subreg:SI (reg:DI 143) 0)
       (subreg:SI (reg:DI 144) 0)))
Failed to match this instruction:
(set (reg:DI 148 [ _4 ])
   (ior:DI (sign_extend:DI (reg:SI 141 [ _4 ]))
       (const_int 32768 [0x8000])))

If we just split it differently we'd get better code because rv64 has sign
extending arithmetic.

So this patch also introduces a set of generic splitters meant to split the
right operations at the SIGN_EXTEND point and voila regression fixed.  It
covers the major W form instructions (add, sub, shifts, rotates, multiply &
divide).  This is generic and is likely to help in tiny ways elsewhere too.

Assisted-By: LLM (Claude) for discovery and testcase generation.

Bootstrapped and regression tested on the c920, K3 is still spinning on K1 is
queued.  Also regression tested on riscv64-elf and riscv32-elf.   Pushing to
the trunk.

	towards IOR.
	* config/riscv/bitmanip.md (ior of sign extended operation): New
	splitters.  Add splitter for setting a single bit via bseti when
	the object being modified has a zero at that bit.

update.title: [RISC-V] Add splitter to enable narrowing load in a load->shift->store sequence
update.body:
I'm not terribly happy with this case.

The basic idea here is we're seeing a load into a wider mode like SI, a right
shift by 8 positions, then a narrow store of that result (HI).

If the target supports fast unaligned access, then that's just a HI load
followed by a HI store.  Obviously this generalizes and appears to be a
run-of-the-mill 3->2 splitter.  Combine is able to simplify the sequence from
the wide load, shift, narrow store to just a narrow load + narrow store.  It
takes care of adjusting the address, mode switches, etc.  So the matching rtl
is just:

(set (mem) (mem)).

That's both the beauty and worry I have.  It's great that combine was able to
see through the sequence and boil it down to its essence, but at that the same
time that leaves us with a splitter that matches much more generally than I
would have preferred.

Checking volatile on the source operand is critical since the load itself gets
narrowed.  I couldn't convince myself that the same couldn't (in theory) happen
with the destination operand if it were being stored back to a location and
only changed a subset of bytes from a prior known value.  So while it's
probably not strictly necessary today, better safe than sorry.

Another 13M (drop in the bucket) dynamic instructions gone.

Bootstrapped and regression tested on K3 and c920, K1 in flight.  Also
regression tested on riscv64-elf and riscv32-elf.  Pushing to the trunk.

	* config/riscv/riscv.md (load->store splitter): New splitter for capturing
	narrowing loads in load -> shift -> narrow store sequence.

update.title: c, c++, middle-end, i386: Introduce __builtin_clmulg builtin [PR128111]
update.body:
The https://wg21.link/P3642R7 paper proposes to add std::clmul and
std::widening_clmul function templates.  Because many targets have
instructions to implement some cases of the carry-less product in
hardware and there are various optimizations only the compiler can do
and lots of different ways to open code it in the source, I think we
need a builtin and pattern matching is of limited use.
Now, clang added __builtin_elementwise_clmul builtin for this, but
1) we don't have any __builtin_elementwise_* builtins so far and no
   agreement on those
2) the builtin only provides type-generic scalar (and vector)
   T = clmul (T, T) operation, but many targets actually have
   instructions to perform widening clmul (e.g. x86 64x64->128,
   etc.), and because std::widening_clmul needs the latter, I think
   it is useful to have a builtin that can handle both
So, the following patch introduces a __builtin_clmulg builtin instead,
if we ever decide to add support of __builtin_elementwise_* builtins
we can certainly add easily support for the clang one as well.
Now, because it is a type-generic builtin, for the widening case
there is a problem that we sometimes don't actually have wider types.
For 32-bit targets without _BitInt there is no type wider than
unsigned long long, for 64-bit targets without _BitInt there is no
type wider than unsigned __int128, for _BitInt target there is no
type wider than unsigned _BitInt(__BITINT_MAXWIDTH__).
So, having a builtin which for 2 arguments of the same type returns
some other type with precision twice as big would only work sometimes.
Instead of this, the builtin has 2 or 3 arguments, as if
  template <__unsigned_integer T>
  T __builtin_clmulg (T, T);
and
  template <__unsigned_integer T>
  T __builtin_clmulg (T, T, T *);
where the former computes the low __builtin_popcountg ((T) ~(T) 0)
bits of the result, while the latter returns the same plus stores
the remaining higher bits of the result to what the third argument
points to (similarly to e.g. __builtin_mul_overflow, except that
__builtin_mul_overflow returns just bool, and accepts arbitrary
set of types, while this one requires all of them to be the same).

Under the hood, this is implemented using two new internal functions,
IFN_CLMUL which returns just the low bits of the result, and
IFN_CLMUL_WIDEN which is similar to IFN_MUL_OVERFLOW etc. in that
it returns COMPLEX_TYPE result with real part being the low half
and imag part being the high half.
As for the implementation, various targets have hw instructions
for some cases of this.
x86 has pclmulqdq (64x64->128) and vcplmulqdq (vector version of that),
arm/aarch64 has some vmul*/pmul* which can do all kinds of stuff
depending on ISA (8x8->8, 8x8->16, 32x32->64, 64x64->128,
powerpc has vpsum* (8x8->16, 16x16->32, 32x32->64, 64x64->128), including
vector in some cases,
riscv has clmul and clmulh (both together can do 32x32->64 resp.
64x64->128 depending on mode, only clmul can do 32x32 resp. 64x64)
and vclmul* to handle vectors,
sparc has xmulx and xmluxhi (64x64->128 together, 64x64 the first),
s390x has vgfm, vgfma (8x8->16, 16x16->32, 32x32->64, 64x64->128).
This patch implements just the x86 part, I'll defer to target maintainers
to do the other arches.

For software implementation fallback, there are various algorithms.
One is the naive O(n^2),
T clmul_naive (T x, T y) {
  T r = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < __builtin_popcountg ((T) ~(T) 0); ++i)
    if ((unsigned) (y >> i) & 1)
      r ^= x << i;
  return r;
}
T2 below is unsigned type with twice the precision of T:
T2 clmul_naive_widen (T x, T y) {
  T2 r = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < __builtin_popcountg ((T) ~(T) 0); ++i)
    if ((unsigned) (y >> i) & 1)
      r ^= ((T2) x) << i;
  return r;
}
another is using Kronecker substitution, depending on maximum number of
active bits in the operands and whether it is the non-widening or widening
case one chooses S in [1, 13] such as for N (precision or max number of
active bits) N <= S * ((1 << S) - 1) (for the widening case) or
N <= S * (1 << S) (for the non-widening one; this is all about how
many additions during the multiplication still don't cause carry over
the given spacing, e.g. for S = 4 0x1111111111111111ULL * 0x11111111ULL
is 0x8888888887654321ULL, so there is no carry over the 4 bits but one
already over the 3 bits, 0x1111111111111111ULL * 0x11111111111111ULL
0xeeedcba987654321ULL so getting closer, and
0x1111111111111111ULL * 0x1111111111111111ULL being
0xfedcba987654321ULL, where there is still no carry over from one group
to another within the least significant 64 bits, but there is one above
that already; unsigned _BitInt(60) can use safely S = 4 even in the
widening case, but unsigned _BitInt(64) only in the non-widening one
and for widening it needs to use S = 5 (where 5 * 5 multiplications
at least if implemented in hw is still better than 4 * 4 * 2),
T clmul_kronecker (T x, T y, int S) {
  T mask = std::bit_repeat ((T) 1, S);
  T xa[S], ya[S], r = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
    xa[i] = x & (mask << i); ya[i] = y & (mask << i);
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
    T t = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < S; ++j)
      t ^= xa[j] * ya[(i + S - j) % S];
    t &= (mask << i);
    r |= t;
  }
  return r;
}
T2 clmul_kronecker_widen (T x, T y, int S) {
  T maskn = std::bit_repeat ((T) 1, S);
  T2 mask = std::bit_repeat ((T2) 1, S);
  T2 xa[S], ya[S], r = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
    xa[i] = x & (maskn << i); ya[i] = y & (maskn << i);
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < S; ++i) {
    T2 t = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < S; ++j)
      t ^= xa[j] * ya[(i + S - j) % S];
    t &= (mask << i);
    r |= t;
  }
  return r;
}
another one is recursive, e.g. adjusted Karatsuba multiplication,
TH is a type with half the precision of T:
T2 clmul_karatsuba_widen (T x, T y) {
  int N = __builtin_popcountg ((T) ~(T) 0);
  TH x0 = x, x1 = x >> (N / 2);
  TH y0 = y, y1 = y >> (N / 2);
  T l = clmul_widen (x0, y0);
  T m = clmul_widen (x0 ^ x1, y0 ^ y1);
  T h = clmul_widen (x1, y1);
  m ^= l ^ h;
  return (((T2) h) << N) | (((T2) m) << (N / 2)) | l;
}
and if we have a non-widening clmul, we can do:
T2 clmul_bitreverse_widen (T x, T y) {
  int N = __builtin_popcountg ((T) ~(T) 0);
  T l = clmul (x, y);
  T h = __builtin_bitreverseg (clmul (__builtin_bitreverseg (x),
                                      __builtin_bitreverseg (y))) >> 1;
  return (((T2) h) << N) | l;
}
The following patch uses all of these algorithms depending on circumstances.
For wi::clmul it uses the naive one, for expansion obviously attempts to
use optabs first and then chooses among the rest.

For _BitInt lowering, it uses an optimized version of the naive one,
while theoretically a recursive algorithm could be best, we don't even
handle normal multiplication that way in libgcc right now.  And from
my benchmarking on x86_64 (see the PR for details), the optimized version
of the naive algorithm consistently beat the Kronecker one when there is
no corresponding hw multiply (while the non-optimized naive was always
slower than the Kronecker substitution).  And the naive one is smallest
in the emitted code.

The patch doesn't add any libgcc libcalls right now, I'm not sure if
we want to do that or not, the problem is that having too many different
cases in libgcc would be code bloat for programs which don't use this,
and choosing just one or two could be too slow in case we only need fewer
bits.  In any case, libgcc libcalls can be added later on, including in
future GCC relelases.

I admit I haven't figured out how the IFNs work with ranges, the only
thing I know is that if the x and y operands have some trailing zeros,
ctz (clmul_widen (x, y)) == ctz (x) + ctz (y), and
clz (clmul_widen (x, y)) == clz (x) + clz (y) + 1.  Not implemented
for now, neither in CCP nor in the ranger.

Possible future optimization might be to lower the two IFNs to their
fallback if optabs are missing, and either let the SLP vectorizer
vectorize it (it doesn't currently) or vectorize it manually,
e.g. the Kronecker substitution algorithm could very well perform some
vector permutations and perform e.g. 4 multiplications at a time, etc.
The paper also talks about the case that clmul (x, x) can be implemented
more efficiently.  And perhaps we could eventually pattern match the
clmul and reversed clmul of reversed args shifted down by 1 as widening
clmul.

The FE changes are mostly following what is done for __builtin_bswapg
or __builtin_bitreverseg already, as similarly to those this is
a type-generic builtin with the return type dependent on the argument
type(s).

update.title: [RISC-V] Add missing splitters for zicond sequences
update.body:
LLVM review of x264 code on RISC-V showed that we were missing splitters for
(LT/LTU & EQ/NE) and (LE/LEU & EQ/NE).  Essentially with the logical AND we can
get the operands in either order and a subset of the splitters didn't have
forms with the two operands reversed.

This adds the two missing splitters.  It should save ~10M instructions on x264
input #1, so pretty tiny, but very clearly an oversight in zicond.md.

tested on the C920 and K3.  K1 is queued.  Pushing to the trunk.

update.title: RISC-V: Extract subvectors via vec_perm_const.
update.body:

implementation is exactly the same as what vec_extract is doing, just
that we're independent of optab modes here and can extract arbitrary

generic handling.  Every possible extract should be just a slidedown.

update.title: [RISC-V] Reorder sequence for (plus (reg) (const_int)) for nontrivial constants
update.body:
Another LLM finding -- more fallout from trying to fix the dhrystone regression
a couple weeks ago.  We very much want to steer PLUS operations where one
operand is a constant through synthesize_add.  The dhrystone fix sent another
class of those into synthesize_add and exposed that the code it generates is
less than ideal.

Basically we generate

  lui
  addi
  add

When adding a large constant to a register.  The lui+add will usually fuse, so
it's often just 2c.  When the result is used in a memory reference it's another
cycle.

  lui+addi
  add
  memref

It can be difficult for fold-mem-offsets to see through this in some cases.  We
can rewrite into

  lui
  add
  addi
  memref

The addi and memref will trivially fold and the lui has no incoming
dependencies.  So practically it's going to be 2-3 cycles instead of 3 cycles.

This saves about 4b instructions in x264 input #1, so north of 2%.  Not bad.
Of course to some degree it's just recovering a recent regression.  So it's not
clear if it's really a net new win or just recovering what we lost.

Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  Bootstrapped on the K3 and C920.  K1 is
in progress.  Pushing to the trunk.

gcc/
	* config/riscv/riscv.cc (synthesize_add): Reorder instructions when we
	do not find a good synthesis.

update.title: RISC-V: Support per-LMUL vector permute cost
update.body:
Turn the scalar permute_cost in common_vector_cost into an array indexed
by LMUL (1, 2, 4, 8) to model non-linear permute scaling, defaulting to
quadratic scaling ({1, 4, 16, 64}) for generic cores.

In riscv_builtin_vectorization_cost, return the baseline cost for LMUL 1.
In costs::adjust_stmt_cost, look up the per-LMUL permute cost for
vec_perm.

Regtested on rv64gcv, showed regressions in 4 files:
  - gcc.target/riscv/rvv/autovec/partial/slp-{1,3,5}.c: Prefers vlseg8
    because generic segment cost is too cheap (1).
  - gcc.target/riscv/rvv/autovec/vls/bswap16-0.c: bswap16 is costed as
    vec_perm, so quadratic scaling avoids large LMUL.

I leave testcases untouched for now.
  - For slp-{1,3,5}.c, will introduce a segment cost table in a separate
    patch.
  - For bswap16-0.c, currently we can't tell if it's a cheaper perm.
    Robin is working on vect; once that allows us to do fine-grained
    permute costing, this can be refined into dedicated cost tables for
    gather/slide/compress.  After that this can be fixed.

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* config/riscv/riscv-protos.h (struct common_vector_cost): Change
	permute_cost to array.
	* config/riscv/riscv-vector-costs.cc (costs::adjust_stmt_cost): Look
	up per-LMUL permute_cost for vec_perm.
	* config/riscv/riscv.cc (rvv_vls_vector_cost, rvv_vla_vector_cost)
	(xt_c9501_vls_vector_cost): Update permute_cost.
	(riscv_builtin_vectorization_cost): Return permute_cost[LMUL_1].

update.title: [committed][PR target/128420] Convert RISC-V define_insn_and_split to simpler define_split
update.body:
LLM review of x264 found a case where we had code like this:

        lui     a5,%hi(tab)
        andi    a4,a0,3
        addi    t0,a5,%lo(tab)
        sh2add  t1,a4,t0
        lbu     t2,0(t1)
        andi    a0,a0,3
[ ... ]

Note the two ANDI instructions.  They compute the same value and put it into
two different places.

One is coming from a define_insn_and_split and thus we don't see it early
enough to have any chance of optimizing it away.  Turning that pattern into a
simple define_split doesn't fix the problem, but it is a necessary step and it
fits into the long term desire to avoid define_insn_and_split when we can.

Implemented thusly.  Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  Bootstrap on K3
and C920 in flight.  K1 is queued.  Pushing to the trunk.

	PR target/128420
gcc/
	* config/riscv/bitmanip.md (andi_add.uw): Turn into define_split.

update.title: [RISC-V] Improve saturating truncation sequences for RISC-V when Zbb is enabled
update.body:
In addition to machine description scanning for bugs, I've also got LLMs
scurrying around spec data looking for inefficient code generation issues on
RISC-V.  This is a fix for one such finding for x264.  It saves a bit over 600m
instructions x264 input #1 on RISC-V.  So it's not huge, but it's not trivial
either.

We're interested in optimizing the unsigned truncation with saturation path.
So if we're truncating with saturation from DI to QI we're going to end up with
a value 0..255.  We can load up the largest value in the range of the output
mode into a register (255 in this case), then issue a umin instruction.  If the
other input was 0..255, then we get its value, otherwise we get 255.  This
naturally relies of the Zbb extension.

Tackling in combine wasn't really feasible as we often need to see too many
instructions to make the transformation.  I could have tackled in isel with
something conditional on a umin opcode.  But fixing the RISC-V expander was
just too easy :-)

An implementation note.  For DI->SI we sign extend the inputs to match
LOAD_EXTEND_OP in the hope that lets us combine the extension with the memory
load.  Otherwise we zero extend.  Either is valid.  It's a heuristic.  I'm sure
it's not going to be optimal somewhere.

The test verifies the full set of useful sat-trunc cases.  DI->{SI,HI,QI} and
SI->{HI,QI}.  It checks that the optimization fires and there's run tests as
well.  Every case improves by at least 1 instruction.

Assisted-By: Claude for discovery and testcase generation.

Tested on riscv32-elf and riscv64-elf.  Bootstrap & regression tested on K3 and
c920.  Pushing to the trunk.

gcc/
	* config/riscv/riscv.cc (riscv_expand_ustrunc): Generate umin based sequence
	when Zbb is enabled.

gcc/testsuite
	* gcc.target/riscv/ustrunc-zbb-1.c: New test.
	* gcc.target/riscv/ustrunc-zbb-run.c: New test.
	* gcc.target/riscv/ustrunc-zbb.h: New common file for ustrunc tests.

update.title: RISC-V: Document that PR_RISCV_V_SET_CONTROL is unsupported
update.body:
There's really no good way for normal userspace applications to disable
vector: once glibc has installed an IFUNC that uses vector it doesn't
have a viable way to disable vector, at it's not likely anything like
that would ever show up.  As such the only way this sort of call would
ever be viable is to construct a shim binary that handles disabling
vector before re-loading the real traget process.  Constructing that
binary would be a fairly mechanical process, but it doesn't seem there's
any interest in doing it.

If someone was to try to make that work we would still run into glibc
issues around IFUNC probing, as we're not looking at
PR_RISCV_V_SET_CONTROL during IFUNC resolution.  That could be fixed,
but it doesn't seem like anyone is all that interested in the feature.
There have been various discussions about deprecating
PR_RISCV_V_SET_CONTROL in the kernel, and it seems very likely that the
prctl() will de deprecated soon.

Regardless of where things go in the kernel: we don't support
PR_RISCV_V_SET_CONTROL in glibc, so let's just document that.

update.title: RISC-V: Adjust VLS subreg handling.
update.body:
Since the regmode_natural_size changes we'd spill subregs like
 (subreg:V4SI (reg:V8SI) 0)
even though a lowpart subreg is safe in a VLA setting.
This is caused by a mismatch in can_change_mode_class and
regmode_natural_size.

can_change_mode_class doesn't look at the subreg byte but would prohibit
all such subregs because we cannot statically tell whether the inner reg
is a register pair or a larger register.

A better way is to always consider VLS vectors unsplittable but don't
always prohibit them in can_change_mode_class.  That way, lowpart
subregs are still allowed but non-lowpart subregs aren't as they won't
be generated in the first place.

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* config/riscv/riscv.cc (riscv_can_change_mode_class): Don't
	prohibit ambiguous VLS subregs.
	(riscv_regmode_natural_size): Make VLS regs unsplittable when
	the vector size is variable.

update.title: RISC-V: Remove redundant VLA niters check in better_main_loop_than_p
update.body:
In better_main_loop_than_p we keep the current LMUL if the loop NITERS > VF.
Because we try M8 first, this early exit locks in M8 before
compare_inside_loop_cost is called.

In pr113112-3.c (NITERS = 25) the vect dump shows:

  Vector inside of loop cost: 105
  ***** Analysis succeeded with vector mode RVVM8SI
  ...
  Vector inside of loop cost: 49
  ***** Analysis succeeded with vector mode RVVMF2QI
  Comparing two main loops (RVVMF2QI at VF 8 vs RVVM8SI at VF 8)
  Keep current LMUL loop because known NITERS exceed the new VF

Because 25 > 8, we reject RVVMF2QI even though both have VF 8 and
RVVMF2QI has lower inside cost.

Furthermore, this check is redundant with compare_loop_overhead,
which already compares estimated vector loop iterations and branch overhead.

This patch removes it and also fixes the XFAILs in pr113112-3.c.

	* config/riscv/riscv-vector-costs.cc (costs::better_main_loop_than_p):
	Remove redundant VLA niters heuristic.

gcc/testsuite/ChangeLog:

	* gcc.dg/vect/costmodel/riscv/rvv/pr113112-3.c: Remove XFAILs.

update.title: RISC-V: Fix reg overlap for vs1 of the widening float reduction
update.body:
Like the widening integer reduction, the vs1 of the widening float
reduction (aka vfwredosum.vs and vfwredusum.vs) is read with
EEW = 2 * SEW while the vs2 is read with EEW = SEW.  The section 5.2
of the vector spec reserves any encoding in which one vector register
supplies source operands with two or more different EEWs.  Thus, the
vs1 must not fall inside the vs2 register group, but we may have below
asm dump when the vs1 comes from the vs2 register group.

  vfwredosum.vs v4,v4,v5

Take the Wn3 constraint for the operand 4 (aka vs1) of the widening
float reduction.  See below issue of the riscv-isa-manual for more
details.

  https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/issues/2350

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* config/riscv/vector.md: Take the Wn3 constraint for the
	operand 4 of the widening float reduction.

update.title: c++: let the target see the attributes that wait for instantiation
update.body:
cplus_decl_attributes splices the late attributes out before calling
decl_attributes, so targetm.insert_attributes never sees them on the
template.  On RISC-V this drops the psABI ABI tag when the function type
is dependent:

```c++
template <typename T> __attribute__((riscv_vls_cc(128))) void a (T) {}
```

a<int> mangles as _Z1aIiEvT_ instead of _Z1aB16riscv_vls_cc_128IiEvT_.

Call the hook before the splice instead.  A template declaration now goes
through the hook twice.

gcc/cp/ChangeLog:

	* decl2.cc (cplus_decl_attributes): Call targetm.insert_attributes
	before the late attributes are spliced out of the list.

gcc/testsuite/ChangeLog:

	* g++.target/riscv/mangle-vls-cc.C: Expect the tag on a template
	whose type is dependent.

update.title: RISC-V: Mangle the ABI tag of a standard calling convention variant
update.body:
The RISC-V psABI[1] says a function using a standard calling convention variant has
to append an extra ABI tag to its mangled name, following the "ABI tags"
rule of the Itanium C++ ABI.  The only variant listed so far is the
fixed-length vector calling convention, whose tag is
riscv_vls_cc_<ABI_VLEN>:

```c
__attribute__((riscv_vls_cc(128))) void foo();
```

now mangles as _Z3fooB16riscv_vls_cc_128v.

[1] "Name Mangling for Standard Calling Convention Variant" in
https://github.com/riscv-non-isa/riscv-elf-psabi-doc/blob/master/riscv-elf.adoc

gcc/ChangeLog:

	* config/riscv/riscv.cc (riscv_get_vls_cc_attr): Let CHECK_ONLY
	suppress the diagnostic only, not the validity test.
	(riscv_lookup_vls_cc_attribute): New function.
	(riscv_vls_cc_function_abi): Use it, and take the arguments from
	the attribute that was found.
	(riscv_abi_tag_present_p): New function.
	(riscv_insert_attributes): New function.
	(TARGET_INSERT_ATTRIBUTES): Define.

gcc/testsuite/ChangeLog:

	* g++.target/riscv/mangle-vls-cc.C: New test.

update.title: RISC-V: Avoid vsetvl insertion on shared table edges [PR middle-end/126236]
update.body:
Late vsetvl PRE can insert a configuration on an edge from a shared
jump-table dispatch.  Such an edge cannot be split for one dispatch
without also changing the other users of the table.

Keep the local configuration in blocks with incoming shared-table edges,
using the existing invalid_opt_bb_p check.

RISC-V shares jump tables, and without this patch the new test fails with
an ICE in rtl_split_edge.  With it, the test passes at VLEN 128 and 256.
The test also checks that its dispatches share their tables.

gcc/ChangeLog:

	PR middle-end/126236
	* config/riscv/riscv-vsetvl.cc (invalid_opt_bb_p): Keep local
	configurations in blocks with incoming shared-table edges.

gcc/testsuite/ChangeLog:

	PR middle-end/126236
	* gcc.target/riscv/rvv/vsetvl/pr126236.c: New test.

Signed-off-by: Kyrylo Tkachov <ktkachov@nvidia.com>
